metadata.title: MCP Integration.
metadata.purpose: Take apart MCP integration for a Claude Code plugin: explain the four transports, the two places the declaration can live, and the literal-string tool-naming template; evaluate the design choices (permissive parser, silent mismatch, wildcard dodge) and name the trade-offs. Land the carry-out that MCP integration is a config entry with an exact connection type and an exact tool name — miss on either and it fails silently.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the exact Asana tool name, mcp__plugin_asana_asana__asana_create_task: exact match fires precisely, one underscore off fires silently, a wildcard also fires but widens scope)

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. 'Add an app' is the wrong mental model — Claude Code has no app installer for a plugin. You edit a config file, declare an MCP server inside it, and pick one of four connection types. So: what actually belongs in that file?

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery. A plugin talks to an external service by declaring it in a config file, and 'declaring' means picking one of four transports — stdio, SSE, HTTP, or WebSocket. These aren't interchangeable; each is a different way to move bytes across the boundary. A local script Claude Code spawns itself talks over stdin and stdout, so it's stdio. A hosted service like Asana lives behind an HTTPS URL and authenticates with OAuth, so it's SSE — a persistent server-sent-events channel. They optimized for honesty about the transport at the expense of one universal setting. Pick stdio for Asana, and Claude never reaches it — no negotiation layer papers over the mismatch.

shot.new_visual_element: One config box branching to four labelled connection types; a mismatched type crossed out, unreachable

production_viz.label: One declaration, four types
production_viz.mechanic: A single config box at top labelled 'external service' branches down into four cards: stdio, SSE, HTTP, WebSocket. A fifth ghost card reading 'one app-install setting' fades in center, gets a terracotta strike through it, and dissolves. Then a local-script icon connects cleanly to the stdio card; a hosted-OAuth icon (Asana) tries to connect to stdio instead, and the line breaks with a small terracotta X before rerouting to SSE, which connects cleanly.

beats.narration_text: Two places that declaration can live, and the choice reveals a priority. A dedicated dot-mcp-dot-json file at the plugin's root — this is what you reach for once you have more than one server, because it scales. Or an inline mcpServers field inside plugin-dot-json — the shortcut for a single simple server. Say Asana lives in dot-mcp-dot-json, type SSE. Now the tool-name convention. The server exposes tools; Claude renames every one of them to a fixed template. mcp, two underscores, plugin, one underscore, the plugin name, one underscore, the server name, two underscores, the tool name. Asana's create-task tool becomes mcp__plugin_asana_asana__asana_create_task — exactly that string, every underscore load-bearing.

shot.new_visual_element: Two config file shapes; THE ANCHOR — the exact tool-name string built piece by piece

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — one exact string
production_viz.mechanic: Two file cards fade in side by side: '.mcp.json' (recommended, multiple servers) and 'plugin.json / mcpServers' (single server). Both fade out. THE ANCHOR. The tool-name string builds left to right in monospace, segment by segment, each segment briefly highlighted as it's named: mcp__ / plugin_ / asana_ / asana__ / asana_create_task, assembling into the full string mcp__plugin_asana_asana__asana_create_task, which then holds, centered, large. THIS EXACT STRING RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Here's the trade-off that string exposes. Claude matches allowed-tools by literal string comparison. Get the name exactly right, and precisely one tool fires — the one you named. Get one underscore wrong, and nothing happens. No error, no strike, no diagnostic — a name that doesn't resolve is indistinguishable from a name the plugin never requested. They optimized for a permissive parser at the expense of a loud failure mode. Some plugin authors dodge that by pre-allowing a wildcard — asana star — which matches every tool the server exposes. That fires without error too. But now the plugin can call anything Asana surfaces: create a task today, delete a project tomorrow, whatever the server adds next release. This works if you value install-time convenience; it fails if the whole point of naming the specific tool was to bound what the plugin could ever do.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the exact string firing cleanly on one tool; then a wildcard string lighting up every tool on the same server

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — exact vs wildcard
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 STRING RETURNS, identical, and fires cleanly into a single lit tool card: 'asana_create_task'. Then one character is swapped (the final underscore run breaks), the string dims, and 'no error. no strike. just silence.' appears beside it in serif italic. Below, a wildcard string 'mcp__plugin_asana_asana__*' appears and lights up every tool card the Asana server offers, all at once, in teal — no error there either, but now the whole row is lit instead of one card.

beats.narration_text: MCP integration isn't an app install — it's a config entry with an exact connection type and an exact tool name. Miss on either, and it fails silently: no exception, no log, just a tool that never fires.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I'm building a Claude Code plugin that needs to create tasks in Asana on the user's behalf. Explain how to wire up the MCP server: which config file the declaration belongs in — a dedicated dot-mcp-dot-json at the plugin root versus the inline mcpServers field inside plugin-dot-json, and when to choose each. Which of the four connection types — stdio, SSE, HTTP, or WebSocket — fits a hosted service that authenticates with OAuth. And the full tool-naming template: mcp, two underscores, plugin, one underscore, plugin name, one underscore, server name, two underscores, tool name — and why every underscore run is load-bearing. Then give me the exact JSON block for a dot-mcp-dot-json entry declaring an Asana server, and the allowed-tools string for calling asana_create_task specifically, not a wildcard. Go deeper: ask the same model what happens on the auth side of an SSE MCP server the first time Claude Code launches — where does the OAuth handshake actually run, does the plugin author or the end user own the client credentials, and what does a silent mid-session token expiry look like to Claude when the refresh quietly fails?
